overview: The Heian period represents the pinnacle of Japanese court culture, producing masterpieces of literature and refined aesthetics. The Fujiwara aristocracy dominated politics while developing uniquely Japanese forms of Buddhism, art and literature.

items.text: Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji, often considered the world's first novel.
Sei Shonagon writes The Pillow Book, a collection of observations and reflections.
Kana syllabaries created, enabling Japanese literature independent of Chinese.
Tendai and Shingon Buddhism develop esoteric practices.
Pure Land Buddhism gains popular following with emphasis on Amida Buddha.
The concept of mono no aware shapes aesthetic sensibility.
Aristocratic life centered on poetry competitions, music, calligraphy and romantic affairs.
Women of the court produced major literary works.
The Tale of Genji remains central to Japanese literature and culture.
The kana writing systems remain fundamental to Japanese language.

fall.text: The Minamoto clan defeated the Taira in the Genpei War, establishing military rule under the Kamakura shogunate.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heian Period
